opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that policy moves slowly, and in a lot of ways it should. People in tech tend to treat that slowness as a bug. But in a democracy, slowness is often the feature that keeps us from writing bad law in a panic. When I was working on policy questions, before I went deep into the technical side, one of the things that struck me was how long even straightforward issues take to work through the system. It takes years, sometimes decades. And that's for issues where everyone roughly agrees on the facts.

With AI, we don't even agree on the facts yet. We don't fully understand how these models work, what they're capable of, or what the right unit of regulation even is. Is it the model? The data? The application? The company deploying it? So I'm actually a little nervous when I see people calling for sweeping legislation right now. Locking in a framework based on today's understanding could cement assumptions that turn out to be wrong in two years. That happens a lot in this field.

The other side of it is that the technology moves on a timescale of months, and policy moves on a timescale of years. You can't close that gap by making policy faster. What you can do is build institutions and expertise in advance. You get technically literate people into government and into agencies. You build relationships between researchers and policymakers before there's a crisis, not during one. Then when the moment comes where action really is needed, you're not starting from scratch.

So I try to be patient about it. I'd rather we spend the next few years building understanding and capacity. Use the authorities that already exist, like consumer protection, civil rights law and liability, which cover a surprising amount of ground. Then we write new rules once we know what we're actually dealing with. Getting it right matters a lot more than getting it first.

r001.rationale: The response says policy moves slowly and that, in a democracy, this slowness can prevent bad laws written in a panic, describing it as a feature rather than a bug.

r002.rationale: It discusses building expertise before a crisis and waiting to write new rules until there is more understanding, but does not say policy must wait for broader societal conditions to become receptive.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that it moves slower than the technology, and I've come to think that's partly by design rather than purely a failure.

When I first started paying attention to policy, coming out of a research background where a paper could go from idea to arXiv in a few months, the pace felt maddening. You'd see a problem clearly, the fix seemed obvious, and then you'd watch two years go by with hearings and comment periods and draft language that never quite got voted on.

What I've come to appreciate is that the slowness is doing some work. Policy is sticky in a way code isn't. If you ship a bad model, you can roll it back next week. If you pass a bad law, you may live with it for a decade, and it shapes what gets built in the meantime. So some friction is a feature. The question is whether the friction is the right kind, whether it's deliberation or just inertia.

The other thing I'd say is that the gap between what policymakers understand and what's actually happening in the field is narrower than people assume, and it's closing. Five or six years ago you'd walk into a congressional office and have to explain what a neural network was. Now the staffers have read the papers, sometimes more carefully than the people citing them. The bottleneck isn't understanding anymore. It's agreeing on what to do, and that's a political problem, not a technical one.

So my mental model is that you shouldn't expect policy to keep pace with the research frontier, and you shouldn't want it to. What you should want is for it to be grounded in what's real rather than what's hypothetical, and to be written in a way that doesn't lock in assumptions that will look silly in three years. That's hard. Most of the time I spend on this is trying to help people write rules that are robust to being wrong about the details, because we are going to be wrong about the details.

r001.rationale: The candidate says policy moves slower than the technology and that this is “partly by design rather than purely a failure.”

r002.rationale: The candidate describes policy delays and political disagreement, but does not say policy change must wait for broader societal conditions to become receptive.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between how long it takes to write a policy and how long it takes to build the understanding and the relationships that make good policy possible. You can write something down very quickly. Getting people to agree on what problem they’re trying to solve, what the government can actually do about it, and what the tradeoffs are—that takes time.

And that’s uncomfortable in AI, because the technology moves so quickly. But I don’t think the answer is simply that policy needs to move at the speed of AI. We need to do the groundwork now: build technical expertise in government, develop ways to evaluate these systems, and establish channels for people to talk to each other. Then, when there’s a reason to act quickly, you’re not starting from zero.

So I tend to think of it as a long-term investment. A conversation that doesn’t produce a bill tomorrow can still be useful if it means that, a few years from now, the people making a decision have a better understanding of what’s at stake.

r001.rationale: The response says building understanding and relationships takes time, but does not state that policy development is slow partly by design.

r002.rationale: It says groundwork can prepare people to act quickly later, but does not say policy change must wait for broader societal conditions to become receptive.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a mismatch between the pace of the technology and the pace of policymaking. And I don’t necessarily mean that as a criticism of policymakers. We want policy to be deliberative. We want people to have a voice in it. But the technology can change substantially while that process is happening.

So I think the question is: what can we do now that will still be useful even if our predictions are wrong? Building technical expertise in government, developing the ability to evaluate these systems, making sure there are channels for researchers and policymakers to talk to each other—those things take time, and they’re valuable across a lot of possible futures. If we wait until we know exactly what the problem is, we may find that we haven’t built the capacity to respond.

r001.rationale: It says policymaking moves more slowly than the technology and explains that policy should be deliberative and give people a voice, indicating the slowness is partly by design.

r002.rationale: It does not say policy change must wait for broader societal conditions to become receptive.
